name: sdsl::bit_vector (SDSL - Succinct Data Structure Library)
claimed_speedup: Project's own description (SDSL 3.0 docs/wiki): sdsl::bit_vector is 'an optimized replacement of the infamous std::vector<bool>'. No numeric benchmark located for this specific claim within the research budget.
stars_or_usage: 2,309 stars; de facto standard succinct-data-structures library, extremely widely cited in the IR/bioinformatics/text-indexing literature (e.g. underlies the SPIRE 2014 sdsl-lite paper and dozens of downstream tools)
tradeoffs: bit_vector itself is a packed bit array similar in spirit to std::vector<bool> but without a standard-library iterator/allocator interface or thread-safety guarantees for concurrent bit writes; the library's real value is the rank/select/compressed layers built on top (rrr_vector, sd_vector, wt_*), which are not literal std::vector<bool>/std::bitset drop-ins and add their own space/time tradeoffs.
caveats: Could not confirm a specific numeric benchmark for bit_vector vs std::vector<bool> within the tool budget for this run; the 'optimized replacement' framing is a first-party claim with no accompanying numbers found, so this is Tier D. Included as this run's one allowed Tier-D entry because the project is unambiguously notable (2.3k stars, foundational in its field). Repository has not been pushed to since 2023-06-02 (>3 years), so maintenance_status is 'abandoned' despite the project's continued heavy citation/usage.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'succinct rank select bit vector github faster than std::vector<bool> C++' -> https://github.com/simongog/sdsl-lite

verification.tier_reason: benchmark_url is null, and no SDSL source compares sdsl::bit_vector against std::vector<bool>: not the README, the benchmark/ suite (FM-index, rrr_vector, wavelet trees, etc.), nor the SDSL arXiv paper 1311.1249. The only 'claim' is misattributed.
verification.notes: Rejected because the record's only evidence belongs to another project (bkille/BitLib, BSD-3-Clause, 76 stars, whose README has Google Benchmark results against std::vector<bool>; worth a separate candidate record). SDSL itself makes no speed claim against a stdlib baseline, though it is notable (2,309 stars). The last commit on default branch master is 2019-12-11; the 2023-06-02 date is the repo pushed_at (a non-default branch). The maintained SDSL v3 is the fork xxsds/sdsl-lite (110 stars), whose README also has no std::vector<bool> claim.

name: Grouped SIMD Hash Table
workload: Single-threaded insert+lookup benchmark with uint64 key/value pairs at up to 2M elements (~80% load factor), including a per-operation (insert / lookup-hit / lookup-miss) breakdown at 1M elements, using SSE2 grouped-metadata probing vs ankerl::unordered_dense's Robin Hood table.
claimed_speedup: At 1M elements: lookup-hit 1.69x faster, lookup-miss 1.21x faster, but insert 0.72x (i.e. ~1.4x slower) than ankerl::unordered_dense. Total wall time roughly ties/edges out ankerl at 1M (71.9ms vs 72.3ms) and 2M (156.3ms vs 157.4ms) elements; ankerl wins clearly at 100k-500k sizes.
tradeoffs: No deletion support, no resizing (fixed capacity, must be pre-sized), SSE2/x86-64 only (no ARM/NEON port), and the insert path is slower than the SOTA baseline it targets -- it only wins on lookup-heavy workloads above ~500k-1M elements.
caveats: Does NOT compare against std::unordered_map at all -- only against martinus/unordered_dense, which is itself already on the KNOWN_LIST as a faster-than-std project, so this is a comparison between two already-fast alternatives, not evidence against the stdlib baseline directly. Result is a narrow/mixed win (loses on inserts, roughly ties on total time). No CPU model stated, capping the tier below A. The README credits an AI 'Deep Research' tool and includes research-log files (INSIGHTS.md, EXPERIMENT_RESULTS.md), suggesting an exploratory/automated project rather than a vetted, independently reviewed library; very new (~9 months) and low-adoption (50 stars).
found_via: gh search repos --topic hashmap --sort stars --limit 20, then gh search repos "hash table" "SIMD" --limit 20

verification.tier_reason: README #results numbers match exactly (1M: 72.3 vs 71.9 ms; 2M: 157.4 vs 156.3 ms; insert 0.72x, hit 1.69x, miss 1.21x), and benchmark_final_sota.cpp plus the g++ command are public. No CPU model is given, so C. The only comparison is against ankerl::unordered_dense, another third-party library. No std::unordered_map or other incumbent is compared anywhere in the repo.
verification.notes: Reject: the only baseline is ankerl::unordered_dense (itself on the known list), which is a third-party library rather than the stdlib/incumbent, and the 'win' is a sub-1% tie on total time. Metadata checks out (MIT, 50 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-12-23).

name: Pairing Heap (priority-queue-testing benchmark suite)
workload: Randomized insert-delete (heap capacity c=1024) and Dijkstra's algorithm on the USA road network, from Larkin/Sen/Tarjan, 'A Back-to-Basics Empirical Study of Priority Queues' (ALENEX 2014).
claimed_speedup: Randomized insert-delete, c=1024: pairing heap 1.00x (fastest) vs implicit-2 (plain binary heap) at 11.87x (i.e. binary heap took 11.87x longer). Dijkstra on USA road map: pairing 1.68x vs implicit-2 3.84x baseline time (~2.3x faster). Sorting: pairing 4.29x vs implicit-2 4.75x (modest win only).
hardware: Dell PowerEdge SC1435, dual AMD Opteron 2212 (dual-core, 2.0GHz, 64KB L1 / 1MB L2 per core), 8GB DDR2-667, Springdale/PUIAS Linux, kernel 2.6.32
stars_or_usage: 2 stars (GitHub mirror of the defunct code.google.com/p/priority-queue-testing, the benchmark suite behind the ALENEX 2014 paper)
tradeoffs: Pairing heap's edge is workload-specific: it dominates on randomized insert-delete and Dijkstra but only modestly beats binary heap on plain sorting, and loses ground on some decrease-key-heavy patterns to other specialized heaps. Comparison is against the paper's own C99 'implicit-2' binary heap (algorithmically identical to std::priority_queue's array-based heap), not literally against libstdc++/libc++'s container.
caveats: 2014-era hardware (AMD Opteron 2212), gcc -O4 with no stated vectorization flags. Repo is an unmaintained auto-export of a shut-down Google Code project, no license file. Paper's headline finding is nuanced -- simple binary heaps remain competitive overall; pairing heap's big wins are specific to certain workloads.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: arXiv export API query -> arXiv:1403.0252 (Larkin, Sen, Tarjan) -> paper cites code.google.com/p/priority-queue-testing -> gh search repositories "priority-queue-testing" found the GitHub mirror

verification.tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed paper (ALENEX 2014, DOI 10.1137/1.9781611973198.7, confirmed via Semantic Scholar). The code is public (driver/trace_driver.c, run_scripts/, Makefile with gcc -O4), and the Opteron 2212 hardware is stated. But the baseline is the authors' own C implicit binary/d-ary heaps, not std::priority_queue or any shipped library, so it is not an A-grade run against the named baseline.
verification.notes: The record's Dijkstra figure was wrong: it compared pairing 1.68 to explicit-2 (3.84), not implicit-2 (1.17), so the claimed ~2.3x Dijkstra win is actually a ~1.4x loss. The entry stays because the paper does show real pairing-heap wins on degenerate and large-heap workloads, but it is a research testbed, not a drop-in library. [orchestrator, user-approved 2026-09-24: rejected; the cited Dijkstra result is a ~1.4x loss vs the implicit binary heap, i.e. the std::priority_queue design]

name: seq::tiered_vector (seq library)
workload: Insertion/deletion of single elements in the middle of the container; project's own qualitative description, no fixed element type/size stated
claimed_speedup: "Several orders of magnitude faster" than std::deque for middle insertion/deletion; project also states sorting a tiered_vector is slower than sorting a std::deque, and iterator-based random access can be slightly slower
tradeoffs: Segmented/tiered layout trades away std::deque's simplicity; the docs themselves say it is explicitly slower than std::deque for sorting and can be slower for pure random-access iteration; interface mimics std::deque but is not a literal drop-in
caveats: "Several orders of magnitude" is a qualitative claim with no exact numbers, workload size, compiler, or CPU model given; no reproducible benchmark artifact with numbers was found for this specific claim; the library's own docs conclude 'you should always benchmark with your own use cases'
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'Thermadiag seq library tiered_vector devector benchmark std::vector std::deque' -> github.com/Thermadiag/seq

verification.tier_reason: docs/tiered_vector.md (current and 2022/2023 revisions) has only the qualitative 'several order of magnitudes faster than std::deque' claim. It gives no timings, sizes, compiler or CPU. benchs/bench_tiered_vector.cpp compares std::vector, std::deque and tiered_vector, but no output from it is published anywhere found.
verification.notes: No numbers for tiered_vector vs std::deque, and the repo has 111 stars (under 1k, not widely referenced), so the rejection is for this record's claim only. Other seq components do have first-party chart benchmarks against std containers: docs/sorted_benchmark.md (seq::flat_set/radix_set vs std::set, i7-10850H, flags unstated). Those could be a separate associative-container record. last_commit corrected to the default-branch (main) commit; 2026-09-21 was pushed_at from another branch.

name: fstring
